power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Hierarchically structured data are common in behavioral and social science research, yet ignoring nested structures can lead to misleading statistical inferences and obscure meaningful variation in measurement and structural relationships across groups.

Multilevel generalized structured component analysis (GSCA) extends component-based structural equation modeling to hierarchical data by allowing measurement loadings and structural path coefficients to vary across higher-level units while retaining common component weights.
This tutorial introduces two-level GSCA and demonstrates its practical implementation using GSCA Pro, free software with a graphical interface.
Data from 5,014 customers across four corporate chains provide a worked example.

We guide readers through model specification, estimation, fit assessment, and interpretation of average and group-specific measurement and structural parameters, highlighting between-group heterogeneity.

Researchers in the behavioral and social sciences frequently encounter hierarchically structured data, in which individuals are nested within higher-level units or contexts (Hox et al., 2018; Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002; Snijders & Bosker, 2012).
text.formatted: Researchers in the behavioral and social sciences frequently encounter hierarchically structured data, in which individuals are nested within higher-level units or contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Hox et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Snijders & Bosker, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Such structures arise when individual responses are influenced not only by individual characteristics but also by the contexts to which individuals belong.

If this nested structure is ignored, statistical models may fail to account for dependencies among observations within the same higher-level unit, potentially leading to inaccurate standard errors and statistical inferences.
Moreover, when relationships among variables differ across groups or contexts, models that assume common parameters across units may obscure meaningful heterogeneity (Hwang et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Moreover, when relationships among variables differ across groups or contexts, models that assume common parameters across units may obscure meaningful heterogeneity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hwang et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Such heterogeneity may reflect contextual differences in how variables are related, beyond differences in their average levels.
Accordingly, researchers need analytical tools that account for dependencies within higher-level units and allow relevant model parameters to vary across groups or contexts.
These considerations also apply when researchers investigate relationships among theoretical constructs operationalized through multiple observed indicators.

Component-based structural equation modeling is an established approach in the behavioral and social sciences that represents constructs as weighted composites of observed indicators and examines their relationships (Cho et al., 2022 (Cho et al., , 2023;; Hwang et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Component-based structural equation modeling is an established approach in the behavioral and social sciences that represents constructs as weighted composites of observed indicators and examines their relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cho et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cho et al., , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Hwang et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: One such approach, generalized structured component analysis (GSCA; Hwang & Takane, 2004 , 2014), integrates component construction, component-indicator relationships, and structural relationships among components through a unified least-squares criterion.
text.formatted: One such approach, generalized structured component analysis (GSCA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Hwang & Takane, 2004</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">, 2014)</ref>, integrates component construction, component-indicator relationships, and structural relationships among components through a unified least-squares criterion.

text.text: When applied to hierarchical data, such models may therefore need to account for potential variation in measurement and structural relationships across groups.

Multilevel GSCA accommodates such variation by allowing component loadings and structural path coefficients to vary across higher-level units while maintaining common component weights (Hwang et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Multilevel GSCA accommodates such variation by allowing component loadings and structural path coefficients to vary across higher-level units while maintaining common component weights <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hwang et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Because each component is thus formed in the same way in every group, these common weights provide a consistent basis for interpreting groupspecific differences in loadings and path coefficients.
Building on this common basis, multilevel GSCA decomposes group-specific loadings and path coefficients into across-group averages and group-specific deviations.
This allows researchers to examine both general patterns and how these patterns vary across groups or contexts.
The between-group standard deviations of these parameters further quantify the extent of variation in measurement and structural relations across groups.

For example, in the fitnesscenter setting examined in this tutorial, the relationship between service equity and dimensions of service experience, or between service experience and perceived value, may be stronger in some corporate chains than in others.

Accordingly, interpreting average parameters alongside groupspecific results and between-group variability, while considering the grouping structure and model fit, is an important part of applying multilevel GSCA to hierarchical data.
Although multilevel GSCA offers these features, applied researchers may find it difficult to implement and interpret without step-by-step guidance.

The primary aim of this tutorial is to provide practical guidance on implementing multilevel GSCA using GSCA Pro (Hwang et al., 2024), a freely available software program with a graphical user interface that requires no programming.
text.formatted: The primary aim of this tutorial is to provide practical guidance on implementing multilevel GSCA using GSCA Pro <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Hwang et al., 2024)</ref>, a freely available software program with a graphical user interface that requires no programming.

text.text: GSCA Pro allows researchers to specify models, assign observed indicators to components, perform single-level and multilevel GSCA, and examine model fit and parameter estimates.
To illustrate these procedures, we use a real-world dataset of 5,014 customers from four corporate fitness chains in Spain.

Through a step-by-step worked example, we demonstrate model specification, estimation, and evaluation, as well as the interpretation of average parameters, between-group variability, and group-specific results.
The remainder of this tutorial is organized as follows.
The Method section introduces the key concepts and methodological framework of multilevel GSCA.
The Illustrative Data and Model section describes the empirical dataset and model used for demonstration.
The Tutorial Using GSCA Pro section provides step-by-step guidance on model specification, estimation, and interpretation using GSCA Pro.
Finally, the Concluding Remarks section addresses practical considerations for applying multilevel GSCA to hierarchical data.
Multilevel GSCA extends the standard GSCA framework to accommodate hierarchically structured data in which individuals are nested within higher-level units.

The central innovation of this method lies in modeling nested structure simultaneously in the measurement and structural components, allowing group-specific variation in measurement and structural parameters to be captured rather than assuming common parameters across groups.
This section summarizes these features before the software illustration.
Multilevel GSCA formulates three sub-models: weighted-relation, componentmeasurement, and structural models.
Each sub-model represents a unique aspect of the relations between indicators and components.

Specifically, consider data from G higher-level units (e.g., corporate chains), where group g contains N 𝑔 individuals (e.g., G = 4 chains, with g = 1, …, G and N g customers surveyed within each chain).

Let z ig denote a vector or set of indicators and γ ig a vector of components for an individual 𝑖 in a group g, where each vector may include both individual-level components that vary across i and group-level components that are constant within a group g.
The weighted relation model defines each component γ ig as a weighted sum of their respective indicators z ig as follows: where W is a matrix of weight parameters common to all groups.

In multilevel GSCA, the weight matrix W is constrained to be common across groups by model specification, so that each component is formed in the same way in every group and loadings and path coefficients are compared on a common basis.
For example, when examining whether service equity influences service experience differently across corporate chains, both components are defined identically in all chains.
Consequently, between-group heterogeneity is represented through group-specific loadings and structural path coefficients rather than groupspecific weights.
This constraint is a modeling assumption and should not be interpreted as a formal test of measurement invariance.
As summary indexes of their indicators, components are expected to linearly approximate their respective indicators within each group.
This relation is specified in the componentmeasurement model as follows: where C g is a loading matrix specific to group g and e ig is a vector of errors for z ig .
Each loading represents the strength and direction of the linear association between a component and its indicators within a group.
These loadings are allowed to vary across groups, enabling the component-measurement model to reflect differences in how components approximate indicators differently between groups.
For example, indicators of service experience may load differently across corporate chains with varying service practices.
The relations among components are specified in the structural model as where B g is a matrix of group-specific path coefficients and ζ ig is a vector of structural errors for γ ig .
Each path coefficient represents the strength and direction of the linear association between components within a group.
These path coefficients are allowed to vary across groups to capture differences in structural relations across groups.
For example, the effect of service equity on service experience may differ across corporate chains.
The group-specific parameter matrices C g and B g can be further decomposed as where L and Q represent the parts common to all groups, respectively, and L g and Q g capture group-specific deviations.
These deviations are constrained to sum to zero across groups, ensuring that L and Q correspond to the average loading and path coefficient structures across groups.
In multilevel GSCA, the group-specific deviations are treated as fixed parameters rather than random variables, and thus no distributional assumptions are imposed on them.
The average parameters characterize general patterns in the relations among variables across groups, whereas the group-specific deviations indicate how each group differs from these overall patterns.

For example, an element of Q may represent the average positive path coefficient from service equity to service experience across corporate chains, while the corresponding element of Q g captures how this coefficient differs for a particular chain.
Moreover, the standard deviations of Lg and Qg across groups quantify the extent to which measurement and structural relations vary across groups.
For instance, a large between-group standard deviation in the path coefficient from service equity to wellness suggests that this relationship varies substantially across corporate chains.

Consequently, once all model parameters are estimated, multilevel GSCA provides estimates of common weights W, average loadings L, average path coefficients Q, betweengroup standard deviations of groupwise loadings and path coefficients, along with group-specific results C g and B g .

These outputs allow researchers to examine heterogeneity between groups directly, identify clusters of groups with similar patterns, or detect units where measurement or structural relations diverge substantially from the overall pattern.

Multilevel GSCA estimates parameters by minimizing a single least-squares criterion that measures discrepancies between observed indicator matrices and their model-implied reconstructions under certain constraints.

Let Z g denote the data matrix of indicators for group g and Γ g the corresponding matrix of component scores, defined as Γ g ≡ Z g W. The least-squares criterion 𝜙 can be expressed as where SS(•) denotes the sum of squared elements.

This formulation shows that multilevel GSCA estimates components and relevant parameters such that the components jointly explain the scores for their indicators and other components as much as possible.
An alternating least-squares algorithm is used to minimize this criterion.

Once parameters are estimated, statistical inference is conducted via nonparametric bootstrap resampling (Efron, 1979; Jung et al., 2019), which provides bootstrap standard errors (SEs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for parameter estimates.
text.formatted: Once parameters are estimated, statistical inference is conducted via nonparametric bootstrap resampling <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Efron, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Jung et al., 2019)</ref>, which provides bootstrap standard errors (SEs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for parameter estimates.

text.text: Estimates are considered statistically significant at the 5% level when their 95% CIs exclude zero.
This approach does not rely on distributional assumptions such as multivariate normality and is therefore well aligned with GSCA.
In GSCA Pro, the default number of bootstrap samples is 100.

However, using more bootstrap samples can reduce Monte Carlo variability in SEs and CIs, and 1,000 or more samples may be preferable when greater numerical stability is needed (e.g., Cho & Hwang, 2024).
text.formatted: However, using more bootstrap samples can reduce Monte Carlo variability in SEs and CIs, and 1,000 or more samples may be preferable when greater numerical stability is needed (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Cho & Hwang, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Multilevel GSCA provides indices for assessing overall model fit and predictive performance, including FIT and out-of-bag prediction error (OPE; Cho et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Multilevel GSCA provides indices for assessing overall model fit and predictive performance, including FIT and out-of-bag prediction error (OPE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Cho et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: FIT quantifies the explanatory power of the model as follows:
Its value represents the proportion of variance in both indicators and components reproduced by the model.
For instance, a FIT of 0.78 indicates that the model explains 78% of the variance in the indicators and components.
The FIT value ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater explanatory power.
In contrast, OPE evaluates the model's predictive performance on unseen observations using an out-of-sample validation procedure.
It represents the model's prediction error relative to Separate local-fit indices can be used to assess measurement and structural models.

The measurement-model fit, denoted by FITM, reflects how well the measurement model reproduces its indicators, whereas FITS evaluates how well the structural model accounts for variance in the components.
Similarly, OPEM and OPES assess the predictive performance of the measurement and structural models, respectively, relative to their corresponding null models.
These indices enable researchers to diagnose whether sources of misfit arise primarily from measurement or structural specification.
To demonstrate the practical implementation of multilevel GSCA using GSCA Pro, we use a survey dataset of 5,014 individuals from 53 fitness centers affiliated with four corporate chains in Spain.
The survey includes multiple indicators measuring perceived service equity, service experience, and service value.
For the empirical illustration, we consider a two-level multilevel GSCA model in which individual customers constitute Level 1 and corporate chains constitute Level 2.
The four corporate chains (G = 4) comprise 2,955, 1,310, 643, and 106 customers, respectively.
This specification allows measurement loadings and structural path coefficients to vary across corporate chains while retaining common component weights.
The resulting analysis provides a worked example of how to specify, estimate, and interpret average and chain-specific measurement and structural parameters using GSCA Pro.
The empirical illustration examines relationships among perceived Service Equity, Service Experience, and Service Value.

Service Equity refers to customers' perceptions of fairness and consistency in service delivery, whereas Service Experience captures their subjective reactions to service encounters (Kumar et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Service Equity refers to customers' perceptions of fairness and consistency in service delivery, whereas Service Experience captures their subjective reactions to service encounters <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Kumar et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Service Value represents customers' overall assessment of the benefits received relative to the sacrifices involved (Zeithaml, 1988).
text.formatted: Service Value represents customers' overall assessment of the benefits received relative to the sacrifices involved <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Zeithaml, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these constructs reflect the roles of perceived fairness and service experiences in shaping customers' evaluations of service value (Martelo-Landroguez et al., 2015; Payne et al., 2008). evaluations of the services relative to their cost, together with satisfaction, positive word-ofmouth, and loyalty intentions.
text.formatted: Together, these constructs reflect the roles of perceived fairness and service experiences in shaping customers' evaluations of service value <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Martelo-Landroguez et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Payne et al., 2008)</ref>. evaluations of the services relative to their cost, together with satisfaction, positive word-ofmouth, and loyalty intentions.

text.text: All five constructs included in the illustration-Service Equity, Wellness, Escape of Routine, Sense of Control, and Service Value-are modeled as components within the GSCA framework.

In component-based structural equation modeling, constructs are treated as weighted composites of observed indicators that behave as unified entities representing the underlying concept (Hwang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In component-based structural equation modeling, constructs are treated as weighted composites of observed indicators that behave as unified entities representing the underlying concept <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hwang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Under this specification, each construct summarizes the information contained in its indicators and is represented by a component score used in the structural analysis.

Three additional observed variables-gender, age group, and membership fee (in euros)-are included as individual-level (Level 1) covariates, each specified as a single-indicator component in the model.
Across the sample, 41.2% of respondents were male and 58.8% were female.
Membership fees averaged €53.20 (SD = 26.10; range = €0-€450).
The largest age group was 41-50 years (n = 1,554), followed by 31-40 (n = 1,388), 50 or older (n = 1,095), 20-30 (n = 912), and under 20 (n = 65).
Descriptive statistics are summarized in Table 2.
text.formatted: Descriptive statistics are summarized in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">2</ref>.

text.text: Membership fee is in euros (€). three dimensions of Service Experience (Wellness, Escape of Routine, and Sense of Control), and Service Value.

The model illustrates how fairness in service delivery may shape customers' experiences, which in turn contribute to their evaluations of service value (Lusch & Vargo, 2006; Olsen & Johnson, 2003; Vargo & Lusch, 2004).
text.formatted: The model illustrates how fairness in service delivery may shape customers' experiences, which in turn contribute to their evaluations of service value <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lusch & Vargo, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Olsen & Johnson, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Vargo & Lusch, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Customers who perceive service delivery as fair and consistent may report more positive emotional and experiential responses.
The model therefore specifies positive paths from Service Equity to Wellness (H1a), Escape of Routine (H1b), and Sense of Control (H1c).
These experiential dimensions, in turn, may contribute to customers' evaluations of service value.

Research on experiential consumption suggests that value judgments reflect not only objective service attributes but also the emotional and experiential benefits derived from service consumption (Prahalad & Ramaswamy, 2004).
text.formatted: Research on experiential consumption suggests that value judgments reflect not only objective service attributes but also the emotional and experiential benefits derived from service consumption <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Prahalad & Ramaswamy, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the model specifies hypothesized positive paths from Wellness (H2a), Escape of Routine (H2b), and Sense of Control (H2c) to Service Value.

Gender, age group, and membership fee are included as Level 1 covariates, with structural paths specified from each variable to Service Value to account for differences in service evaluations associated with demographic characteristics and membership costs.
Theoretical Model of the Service Equity-Service Experience-Service Value Framework Note.
The theoretical model specifies that Service Equity predicts the three dimensions of Service Experience-Wellness, Escape of Routine, and Sense of Control-which in turn predict Service Value.
Gender, age group, and membership fee were included as covariates predicting Service Value to account for demographic and contextual variability.

This section provides a step-by-step demonstration of multilevel GSCA using GSCA Pro (version 1.3.2), freely available at https://www.gscapro.com/, where readers can download the software and access the user manual and related publications.
text.formatted: This section provides a step-by-step demonstration of multilevel GSCA using GSCA Pro (version 1.3.2), freely available at <ref type="url" target="https://www.gscapro.com/">https://www.gscapro.com/</ref>, where readers can download the software and access the user manual and related publications.

text.text: The analysis proceeds through five stages: importing the dataset, selecting the higher-level grouping variable, specifying the component-measurement and structural models, configuring and running estimation, and interpreting the results.
Figures 2-11 illustrate the corresponding steps in GSCA Pro.
After installing and launching GSCA Pro, users can begin by clicking the New Project button (house-shaped icon) in the upper-left corner of the main interface.
This opens the New Project dialog (Figure 2), where users enter a project name, select the dataset using the File button, and specify a location to save the project.
text.formatted: This opens the New Project dialog (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>), where users enter a project name, select the dataset using the File button, and specify a location to save the project.

text.text: Users should also indicate whether the first row contains variable names and select the appropriate delimiter for the data file.
After confirming these settings, click OK to create the project.
Once the data are imported, users can inspect the dataset in the Data window (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Once the data are imported, users can inspect the dataset in the Data window (Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>).

text.text: GSCA Pro has three main workspaces, accessible through the tabs in the lower-right corner:
Data, for inspecting observations and variables; Model, for specifying component-measurement and structural models; and Result, for examining estimates and other output after running the analysis.
Users can switch between these workspaces as they proceed through the analysis.
Figure 3
To initiate multilevel GSCA, select Analysis → GSCA → Multilevel GSCA from the top menu.
A dialog window then asks for the grouping variable that identifies the Level-2 unit (Figure 4).
text.formatted: A dialog window then asks for the grouping variable that identifies the Level-2 unit (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>).

text.text: The dialog lists all variables in the dataset, including chains, which identifies the four corporate chains (G = 4).
For the present analysis, select chains and click OK to proceed to the Model window, where the component-measurement and structural models can be specified.

Selection of the Grouping Variable in Multilevel GSCA Specifying the Measurement and Structural Models Model specification in GSCA Pro involves two main steps: defining the componentmeasurement model by assigning indicators to components and specifying the structural model by drawing paths among components.
Both steps are performed in the Model window, following the component definitions and structural relationships described in the previous section.
To specify the component-measurement model, select Add Component from the toolbar on the left and click on the modeling canvas to add a component, represented by a hexagon (Figure 5).
Next, double-click the component to open the indicator-assignment dialog (Figure 6), where users can enter a component name and select its corresponding observed indicators.
For example, enter Service Equity as the component name and assign indicators SE1-SE6.

Repeat this procedure for Wellness, Escape of Routine, Sense of Control, and Service Value using the  Adding Components to the Model Canvas in GSCA Pro Assigning Indicators to a Component in GSCA Pro Next, specify the structural model by selecting Add Path from the left toolbar.
To create a directional path, click first on the predictor component and then on the outcome component.
Following the theoretical model in Figure 1, draw paths from Service Equity to Wellness, Escape of Routine, and Sense of Control, and from each of these three components to Service Value.
text.formatted: Following the theoretical model in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>, draw paths from Service Equity to Wellness, Escape of Routine, and Sense of Control, and from each of these three components to Service Value.

text.text: Add paths from gender, age group, and membership fee to Service Value.
Figure 7 shows the completed structural model in the GSCA Pro Model window.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">7</ref> shows the completed structural model in the GSCA Pro Model window.

text.text: The Model Window in GSCA Pro Displaying the Fully Specified Multilevel GSCA Model
Once the model is fully specified, click the Preference button in the upper-right toolbar to open the Estimation Options dialog (Figure 8).
text.formatted: Once the model is fully specified, click the Preference button in the upper-right toolbar to open the Estimation Options dialog (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">8</ref>).

text.text: This dialog allows users to configure estimation settings, including the maximum number of iterations, convergence tolerance, the number of bootstrap samples, and missing-data handling options.
Detailed explanations of these settings are available in the GSCA Pro user manual.

For this tutorial, we used 200 bootstrap samples to obtain bootstrap standard errors and confidence intervals for illustrative purposes rather than as a general recommendation for inferential precision.
Particular caution is warranted when interpreting bootstrap intervals for group-specific estimates based on very small groups or summaries of heterogeneity across only a few higher-level units.
Estimation Options for Multilevel GSCA in GSCA Pro After confirming the estimation settings, click the Run button in the upper toolbar to estimate the model.
GSCA Pro then displays the Result window (Figure 9), which reports model fit and prediction indices, component weights, and parameter estimates for the measurement and structural models.
Users can access the complete output by selecting View Full Result from the left-side panel.

The results are examined in the following order: (1) overall model fit and predictive performance; (2) component weights, average loadings, and between-group variation in measurement parameters; (3) average structural path coefficients and between-group variation; (4) covariate effects; and (5) group-specific path coefficients.
Table 3 summarizes average path coefficients, between-group variability, and group-specific estimates for the structural relationships, including covariate paths.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">3</ref> summarizes average path coefficients, between-group variability, and group-specific estimates for the structural relationships, including covariate paths.

text.text: The complete GSCA Pro output, including the measurement-model estimates, is provided in the Supplementary Material.   S6 of Supplementary Material.
text.formatted: The complete GSCA Pro output, including the measurement-model estimates, is provided in the Supplementary Material.   <ref type="table">S6</ref> of Supplementary Material.

text.text: GSCA Pro reports several indices for evaluating overall model fit and predictive performance, along with separate indices for the measurement and structural models (Figure 11).
text.formatted: GSCA Pro reports several indices for evaluating overall model fit and predictive performance, along with separate indices for the measurement and structural models (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">11</ref>).

text.text: The fitted model yields FIT = .636, indicating that it accounts for 63.6% of the total variance in the indicators and components, with an adjusted FIT (AFIT) of .636.
The measurement model explains 74.9% of the indicator variance (FITM = .749), whereas the structural model explains 22.6% of the component variance (FITS = .226).
For predictive performance, the overall out-of-bag prediction error (OPE) is .366, indicating lower prediction error than the null model based on sample means.
The local prediction indices also indicate lower prediction errors than their respective null models for both the measurement model (OPEM = .252) and the structural model (OPES = .777).
These results illustrate how GSCA Pro can be used to evaluate in-sample fit and out-of-sample predictive performance separately.
As described in the Method section, multilevel GSCA estimates common component weights (W), average loadings (L), and average structural path coefficients (Q).
GSCA Pro reports these estimates along with their bootstrap SEs and 95% CIs (Supplementary Material, Tables S2-S4).
text.formatted: GSCA Pro reports these estimates along with their bootstrap SEs and 95% CIs (Supplementary Material, Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S2-S4</ref>).

text.text: With corporate chains as the Level 2 unit, all estimated weights for the multipleindicator components have 95% CIs excluding zero, indicating that each indicator contributes to the formation of its corresponding component.

Across the four corporate chains, the average loadings are positive and statistically significant for all indicators, with most showing relatively strong associations with their respective components.
For example, the Service Equity loadings range from .847 to .924, while those for Service Value range from .802 to .946.
The three Service Experience dimensions also exhibit generally high loadings, although some indicators show weaker associations.
Overall, these results indicate that the components are generally well represented by their indicators.

The between-group standard deviations (SDs) of group-specific loadings are relatively small for most indicators (.007-.066), suggesting limited variation in measurement relationships across chains (Supplementary Material, Table S5).
text.formatted: The between-group standard deviations (SDs) of group-specific loadings are relatively small for most indicators (.007-.066), suggesting limited variation in measurement relationships across chains (Supplementary Material, Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: Although the reported bootstrap 95% CIs exclude zero, the estimated SDs are small relative to the corresponding average loadings.
This pattern is consistent with relatively similar measurement structures across the four corporate chains, potentially reflecting common branding and service delivery practices.

The average structural path coefficients indicate positive and statistically significant relationships between Service Equity and all three dimensions of Service Experience: Wellness (β = .631, 95% CI [.593, .678]), Escape of Routine (β = .679, 95% CI [.645, .727]), and Sense of Control (β = .586, 95% CI [.541, .652]).
However, the relationships between these dimensions and Service Value differ considerably.

Escape of Routine shows the strongest positive relationship with Service Value (β = .705, 95% CI [.624, .775]), followed by a smaller but statistically significant relationship for Wellness (β = .126, 95% CI [.040, .200]).
In contrast, the path from Sense of Control to Service Value is not statistically significant (β = -.033, 95% CI [-.121, .078]).
Thus, although Service Equity is positively associated with all three experiential dimensions, these dimensions differ in their relationships with perceived Service Value.

The between-group SDs of structural path coefficients are modest for the Service Equity → Service Experience paths (.078-.094) and smaller for the Service Experience → Service Value paths (.008-.035; Supplementary Material, Table S6).
text.formatted: The between-group SDs of structural path coefficients are modest for the Service Equity → Service Experience paths (.078-.094) and smaller for the Service Experience → Service Value paths (.008-.035; Supplementary Material, Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>).

text.text: Although the reported bootstrap 95% CIs exclude zero, these results indicate relatively limited between-chain variation, particularly in the paths linking Service Experience to Service Value, while allowing for differences in individual chain-specific coefficients.

Among the covariates, Gender had a small but statistically significant positive relationship with Service Value (β = .038, SE = .018, 95% CI [.005, .070]), indicating that female customers (coded 2) reported slightly higher perceived service value than male customers (coded 1), on average, after accounting for the other variables in the model.

Membership Fee showed a statistically significant negative relationship with Service Value (β = -.086, SE = .021, 95% CI [-.137, -.053]), indicating that customers paying higher membership fees tended to report lower perceived service value, consistent with cost-benefit considerations underlying value evaluations.
Age was not significantly associated with Service Value under the ordered age-group coding (β = .026, SE = .020, 95% CI [-.012, .064]), after accounting for the other variables in the model.
In an ancillary single-level analysis that ignores the nested structure, Age appeared significant (β = .051, SE = .008, 95% CI [.037, .067]).
The single-level model yielded a smaller standard error than the multilevel model, although the two specifications differ in how they account for groupspecific parameter variation.

The multilevel results also show variation in the Age coefficient across chains (group-specific β = -.051 to .062; Table 3), highlighting between-chain differences that are not captured by the pooled single-level estimate.
text.formatted: The multilevel results also show variation in the Age coefficient across chains (group-specific β = -.051 to .062; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">3</ref>), highlighting between-chain differences that are not captured by the pooled single-level estimate.

text.text: Multilevel GSCA also provides group-specific parameter estimates, which show how each group differs from the average pattern.

Because the measurement model showed limited between-group variation (see Common and Average Model Parameters), we focus here on the group-specific path coefficients reported in Table 3 (see also Supplementary Material, Tables S12-S15).
text.formatted: Because the measurement model showed limited between-group variation (see Common and Average Model Parameters), we focus here on the group-specific path coefficients reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">3</ref> (see also Supplementary Material, Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S12-S15</ref>).

text.text: These estimates provide descriptive information that complements the average coefficients and between-group SDs, rather than formal tests of differences between groups.
The paths from Service Equity to all three dimensions of Service Experience were positive and statistically significant in all four chains, with differences primarily in magnitude.

Chain 3 showed the largest coefficients for Wellness (β = .755, 95% CI [.669, .847]), Escape of Routine (β = .837, 95% CI [.765, .908]), and Sense of Control (β = .714, 95% CI [.641, .794]), whereas Chain 4 showed the smallest (β = .507, .593, and .504, respectively).
These results
Experience varies across organizational contexts.
The paths from Service Experience to Service Value generally followed the average pattern.
Escape of Routine was positively and significantly associated with Service Value in all four chains (β = .675-.765).
Wellness showed smaller positive coefficients that were statistically significant in Chains 1-3 (β = .115-.136).
In Chain 4, the estimate was similar in magnitude (β = .122) but had a wider 95% CI [-.227, .435], which included zero.
This illustrates the lower precision of estimates for Chain 4, the smallest chain (n = 106).
Sense of Control was not significantly associated with Service Value in any of the four chains (β = -.074 to .019), consistent with its non-significant average coefficient.

Overall, these group-specific results are consistent with the between-group SDs, showing relatively modest variation in the Service Equity → Service Experience paths and smaller variation in the Service Experience → Service Value paths.
They also illustrate why groupspecific coefficients should be interpreted alongside their CIs and group sizes, particularly when the number of observations differs substantially across groups.
This tutorial introduced the conceptual foundations of multilevel GSCA and demonstrated its implementation in GSCA Pro through a real-world example.

Multilevel GSCA extends component-based structural equation modeling to hierarchically structured data by allowing measurement loadings and structural path coefficients to vary across groups while retaining common component weights.

We provided step-by-step guidance for specifying and estimating a two-level GSCA model, evaluating its model fit and out-of-sample predictive performance, and interpreting average and group-specific parameter estimates.

By connecting these methodological concepts with a practical software demonstration, we hope this tutorial will serve as an accessible resource for researchers seeking to apply component-based structural equation modeling to hierarchical data across diverse behavioral and social science settings.
